What's moving the market: Singapore's biggest property deals and hottest searches (Oct 30)
article:
Here is this week’s data-led look at Singapore’s property market, covering record transactions, rental benchmarks and the most searched homes on EdgeProp.

The following insights are compiled from EdgeProp Buddy , URA Realis and data.gov.sg, downloaded as of Oct 28.

Non-landed private homes — new launches, resales and rents

The priciest condo unit transacted over the fortnight ending Oct 28 was at Tomlinson Heights , resold for $14.8 million or $3,657 psf on Oct 15. The sixth-floor apartment has five bedrooms and measures 4,047 sq ft in total floor area. The freehold condo is situated just off Orchard Boulevard.

Coming in second on the list of highest-priced condo transactions was the bigger of the two penthouses at newly launched freehold project The Serra Residences in prime District 11. The 2,669 sq ft, five-bedroom unit on the 28th floor fetched over $11.2 million or $4,200 psf.

The Serra Residences, located along Bassein Road, was launched on Oct 16. It has two penthouses — the other is smaller at 2,648 sq ft and does not appear to have been sold based on caveats lodged.

The Serra Residences was also the most transacted new-launch condo in the last fortnight, with 24 deals logged. This was followed by Union Square Residences with eight and Lucerne Grand with seven.

Landed homes — highest transacted prices and rents

In the landed housing segment, a two-storey bungalow along Matlock Rise was resold for nearly $16.4 million, making it the highest-priced landed home transacted during the 14 days to Oct 28. Its unit price works out to $1,607 psf based on the freehold land area of 10,198 sq ft.

Located in Braddell Heights Estate in District 13, the Matlock Rise detached house was marketed for sale by JLL in July with an asking price of roughly $18 million. It has an existing built-up area of more than 5,500 sq ft, but could potentially be redeveloped to span 10,000 sq ft, JLL had said then.

Meanwhile, another detached house, located on Redwood Avenue in the Eden Park estate in Bukit Timah, was resold for $13.96 million on Oct 20. It sits on a freehold plot measuring 5,225 sq ft.

title: Sky Seah on what really makes a property valuable
article:
As a real estate economist, academic and mother, Dr Sky Seah understands why parents are willing to pay a premium for a home near a good school.

She believes that premium will endure as long as proximity improves the chances of admission, parents continue to place a high value on primary education, and households prefer to minimise commuting distances.

Seah, senior lecturer in the Department of Real Estate, National University of Singapore (NUS), views the Ministry of Education’s move to increase the number of places available under Phase 2C of the Primary 1 registration exercise as a positive step towards broadening the socioeconomic composition of popular schools.

However, she doubts it will significantly reduce the premium for homes nearby.

The reason lies in a fundamental economic principle: property prices are determined at the margin.

“The premium really depends on the person who is willing to pay to outbid the other person,” she explains.

As long as there is a sufficiently large pool of buyers with the financial means and willingness to outbid others, Seah believes premiums for sought-after locations will endure.

Looking beyond the freehold premium

In Singapore’s property market, freehold homes have long commanded a premium over their 99-year leasehold counterparts, especially in the traditional prime districts of 9, 10 and 11.

Yet the strong sales of two recent 99-year leasehold condo launches at River Valley Green underscore the appeal of newer leasehold homes, even in prime districts.

In August 2025, Wing Tai Holdings launched the 524-unit River Green , selling 88% of its units over the launch weekend at an average price of $3,130 psf.

In March this year, GuocoLand launched the 455-unit River Modern , with 410 units (90%) snapped up at an average price of $3,226 psf on its opening weekend. Both projects are 95% sold to date.

In addition to being at the doorstep of Great World MRT Station on the Thomson-East Coast Line, these 99-year condos offer a greater value proposition in terms of design, layout and efficiency of the units, says Seah.

“They are also likely to be more energy-efficient and offer modern amenities that meet the evolving expectations of today’s discerning buyers.”

By comparison, older freehold condos in the same neighbourhood may offer larger units, but their layouts and interiors could be dated, facilities more limited and maintenance costs higher.

“Purchasing an older, less efficient unit entails an opportunity cost for both investors and owner-occupiers alike, as physical deterioration and functional obsolescence may lead to higher maintenance costs, reduced rental competitiveness, and diminished quality of life when compared to newer alternatives,” says Seah.

She believes the appeal of newer 99-year leasehold developments reflects the difference between paying a premium for perpetual ownership and paying for the quality of the home itself.

Owners who continue holding ageing properties may also tie up capital that could otherwise be redeployed into newer homes offering a better living environment, she adds.

This does not mean freehold tenure has lost its appeal. Rather, Seah believes buyers are increasingly weighing the benefits of perpetual ownership against factors such as connectivity, efficient layouts, amenities and overall liveability.

Renewal through collective sales

The growing obsolescence of older private residential developments could also prompt more owners to consider collective sales as a means of rejuvenating established neighbourhoods.

“I expect that more people will be thinking about collective sales,” says Seah.

On Sept 8, Parliament passed a Bill to lower the consent thresholds for collective sales of older developments, potentially making redevelopment easier once the changes take effect.

However, Seah points out that individual owners’ circumstances can still complicate collective sales.

In the prime districts, some foreign owners who bought their properties before successive cooling measures took effect may be reluctant to sell, as purchasing a replacement home could expose them to the 60% additional buyer’s stamp duty.

Thus, while redevelopment may make economic sense, securing agreement among owners remains a challenge.

Smaller homes driven by affordability

While newer homes may offer more efficient layouts and modern amenities, Seah believes their increasingly compact sizes reflect another reality of Singapore’s housing market: affordability.

“Space is a normal good,” she says. “The more you can afford, the larger a place you will want.”

In economic terms, a normal good is one for which demand generally increases as income rises. Applied to housing, this suggests that buyers who can afford more space will generally prefer a larger home.

Developers have increasingly turned to smaller units and more efficient layouts to keep overall purchase prices within buyers’ budgets.

Demographic changes — including smaller families, more single-person households and couples without children — have contributed to demand for compact apartments. But Seah believes affordability plays a bigger role.

“I think it is primarily due to budgetary constraints that people have opted for smaller units,” she says.

A flattening price gradient

Beyond the size and design of individual homes, Seah believes that improved transport connectivity is reshaping how buyers value residential locations across Singapore.

The nation remains largely a monocentric city, with major employment centres, established amenities and key transportation hubs concentrated around the city centre, she explains.

This has historically created a price gradient, with homes closer to the city commanding higher prices than those farther away.

However, Seah believes this gradient is flattening as Singapore’s MRT network expands, particularly with the progressive opening of the Thomson-East Coast Line.

The decentralisation of employment to regional hubs and improvements in suburban amenities are also contributing to this shift.

At Bayshore, the 515-unit Vela Bay , which fronts Bayshore MRT Station on the Thomson-East Coast Line, illustrates the appeal of well-connected suburban locations.

Developer SingHaiyi sold 72% of the units at an average price of $2,886 psf at launch in April, setting a new price benchmark for the neighbourhood.

Recent Government Land Sale (GLS) tenders also illustrate the changing price dynamics.

The New Upper Changi Road site, opposite Bedok Mall and the integrated transport hub in the Outside Central Region, attracted a top bid of $1,537 psf per plot ratio (ppr).

Meanwhile, the Lorong Puntong site in the Bishan-Upper Thomson area of the Rest of Central Region (RCR) fetched $1,612 psf ppr.

Both exceeded the $1,243 psf ppr achieved for a prime residential site at Marina Gardens Lane, located in the RCR and fronting Gardens by the Bay. It is also a short walk to the Marina South MRT Station.

While individual land bids reflect site-specific considerations, Seah sees the strong pricing of these well-connected sites outside the city centre as an indication of the flattening price gradient across Singapore’s residential market.

She views this as a positive development, giving households more choices of desirable neighbourhoods beyond the city centre without necessarily sacrificing convenience.

More housing choices in prime locations

Seah also welcomes government efforts to create more diverse housing options in established and prime residential estates such as the former Bukit Timah Turf City and Mount Pleasant.

She believes greater socioeconomic diversity in these neighbourhoods is desirable.

Concentrating wealth in a limited number of districts risks creating residential enclaves where households of similar economic backgrounds live, socialise and send their children to the same schools. More diverse housing options could help counter that tendency, she says.

For Seah, the gradual flattening of Singapore’s residential price gradient reflects a market where improved connectivity, amenities and housing options are making more neighbourhoods desirable places to live.

While sought-after locations will continue to command a premium, buyers increasingly have more choices about where — and how — they want to live.

Dr Sky Seah is a judge at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026

title: Desmond Sim on life after Realion: Lessons from football, music and real estate
article:
Six years ago, a friend took Desmond Sim to a shrine in Kamakura, about an hour south of Tokyo. Known as Zeniarai Benten, it sits in a cave by the side of the road. Visitors walk through a narrow passage built into the rock, which opens into a small valley surrounded by steep cliffs.

At the shrine, visitors wash coins and paper money in sacred spring water to symbolise a doubling of wealth. Sim was in Japan for the Fuji Rock music festival.

Shortly after his return, he was approached to lead ETC (formerly Edmund Tie & Co). He took over as CEO in July 2021.

He returned to the shrine two years ago, while in Japan for the Summer Sonic festival, and performed the same ritual. In February 2025, he became group CEO of Realion Group, the holding company of ETC and OrangeTee.

Following the announcement of his departure from Realion on Sept 17, Sim went to Japan for several indie concerts, including Belle and Sebastian’s 30th-anniversary tour in Tokyo. He has followed the Scottish band since the 1990s.

During the trip, he made sure he visited the shrine in Kamakura and repeated the money-washing ritual. The following morning, he received two prospective job offers, with a third lined up. “I’m not particularly superstitious, but the coincidence was too compelling to ignore,” says Sim.

‘A complete circle’

Sim turned 52 on Oct 3. The number is significant, he says. “It represents a full deck of cards, and there are 52 weeks in a year. I call it a complete circle.”

It felt like the right time to take stock. He and Realion management, he says, were no longer heading in the same direction. Being CEO was a great opportunity, but Sim felt he had become a “glorified human resource person, solving other people’s problems”.

Every job, he acknowledges, involves things one may not enjoy. “But when they outnumber the things you enjoy doing, that’s when you start to think perhaps it’s time to go.”

He is not retiring, though. “I still need a job to service the mortgage on my little home,” he quips. He reckons his next role may not come with a C-suite title.

Instead, he wants to return to the kind of work he did for a decade as CBRE’s head of research for Singapore and Southeast Asia: presenting to clients and advising them.

“When you speak to clients, you’re not just imparting your knowledge,” he says. “You are also learning from them, from their reactions and their questions. I’m always very curious, so I enjoyed that interaction, and it’s something that I have really missed.”

This is not the first time he has chosen this path. Earlier in his career, he left a fund management role at Ascendas after less than two years to return to research at JLL.

The football manager

Sim’s biggest culture shock was the move from CBRE to ETC. “CBRE is such a well-oiled MNC. It’s not about the size, it’s about the operations,” he says. ETC, a homegrown firm, worked very differently.

Real estate, he stresses, is a people business. Rather than expecting everyone to think like him, he learnt to adapt to how the team worked and bring people along. “Being a leader is like that,” he says. “You cannot charge ahead, then turn around and realise no one is behind you.”

He likens being a CEO to managing a football club, and that means knowing what each player is good at. “Even if you have 10 Cristiano Ronaldos in your team and they score 20 goals, if you have a lousy goalkeeper and the opponents score 21, you still lose the game,” says Sim. “So it’s about putting the right people in the right positions.”

From CDs to Spotify

The real estate sector has transformed significantly over the past decade. Sim has had a front-row seat, both as CEO of a real estate advisory firm and as a judge on the panel of the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards for the past four years.

Outside property, there is another industry he knows well: music, as both a fan and a musician. In 1987, while still in secondary school, Sim and his friends formed indie-pop band Lilac Saints, with Sim on drums. The band reunited to perform via Zoom during the Covid lockdown, and in January 2023 performed at a reunion concert, Lilac Saints & Friends, at the Esplanade Recital Studio to celebrate 35 years of friendship.

He sees parallels between the two industries, and his own music collection charts the shift. In the 1990s, he began collecting compact discs (CDs), and even went to Ikea to buy racks to store them. At one point, he switched to Sony’s MiniDiscs for their superior sound quality.

Then came streaming. Today, his CDs sit in boxes in a self-storage unit, and he is considering throwing them away. “I can’t even find a CD player to play them anymore,” he laments.

He sees the same shift in how Singaporeans use their homes. “You don’t need a three-bedder that is 2,000 sq ft anymore,” he says. “[Many] people don’t even watch TV in the living room anymore. They are watching Netflix on their tablets in bed.”

‘Stay curious’

Technology has also changed the real estate agency business and how homes are sold. Sim found that out first-hand when he sold his former home at Castle Green condo in Yio Chu Kang in early 2020.

He first contacted the agent who had handled his purchase of the unit, by then a relatively senior hand. The agent came by, photographed the unit and listed it for sale. Two weeks on, there were still no takers.

Sim then turned to a close friend at a property development firm, who recommended a PropNex agent. “The guy came, took a fly-through video, and sold the apartment in three days,” he relates.

With property portals making information easier to access, “even someone sitting in an igloo in Iceland can find out the latest HDB prices in Singapore”, he says. “All you need is WiFi connectivity. You can’t bluff the client anymore.”

As a former head of research, he is frequently asked whether AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude will one day replace researchers and analysts. His answer is no.

“The same set of data can be interpreted in different ways,” he says. “What makes you a key opinion leader is that you take all this data and formulate your own view. Equally important is knowing your audience and how to communicate those insights effectively. That’s what makes a great presenter or adviser.”

People should not fear AI, he adds. “The most important thing is to remain curious. The day you lose the urge to learn, that’s when you will be displaced.”

As for what comes next, Sim is weighing his options. But with his coins already washed at the shrine, he reckons it is only a matter of time before the right opportunity comes along.

Desmond Sim is a judge at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026

title: Another duplex penthouse at Mon Jervois heads to auction, this time at $4.38 mil
article:
A three-bedroom duplex penthouse at Mon Jervois , a 99-year leasehold luxury condo in District 10, went under the hammer at SRI’s auction on Oct 28. The 2,368 sq ft property was offered via an owner’s sale with a guide price of $4.38 million, or $1,850 psf.

Caveats lodged show that the fifth-floor unit was previously purchased for $4.36 million ($1,841 psf) in September 2022.

The penthouse’s lower level comprises a living and dining area that opens out to a balcony, alongside separate dry and wet kitchens. There is also a junior master bedroom with an en suite bathroom, as well as a common room.

Meanwhile, the upper level houses the master bedroom and a roof terrace. Both the master and junior master bedrooms come with private balconies.

Mok Sze Sze, managing partner of SRI Auction, says the development offers a “tranquil, low-density living environment”. She expects the property to garner interest from homebuyers seeking spacious homes.

This is the second penthouse at Mon Jervois to go under the hammer this year. In September, a larger 2,626 sq ft duplex penthouse at the development was put up for auction by Knight Frank at a guide price of $4.83 million ($1,839 psf).

The property did not sell at auction and was withdrawn. However, it remains available for purchase by private treaty and is currently listed at a lower price of $4.6 million ($1,752 psf).

Located along a cul-de-sac on Jervois Road, just off River Valley Road, Mon Jervois is a 109-unit condo that was completed in 2016. Its five low-rise blocks feature one- to four-bedroom units ranging from 614 to 1,905 sq ft. There are also two- to four-bedroom penthouses sized between 1,475 and 3,003 sq ft.

It is within a 1km radius of Gan Eng Seng Primary School and Alexandra Primary School, while River Valley Primary School, Radin Mas Primary School and Queenstown Primary School are 2km away.

Mon Jervois has recorded just three resale transactions this year.

URA caveats show that the most recent resale deal at the development occurred on May 8, when a 624 sq ft one-bedder on the first floor fetched $1.23 million, or $1,968 psf.

Prior to that, a smaller 614 sq ft, one-bedroom unit was sold for $970,000 ($1,581 psf) on March 17.

The last recorded sale of a three-bedroom duplex penthouse at the development was in November 2022, when a 2,368 sq ft unit fetched about $3.79 million ($1,600 psf).

title: Resale of duplex five-bedder scores $3.58 mil profit at District 10's Tomlinson Heights
article:
A duplex five-bedder at Tomlinson Heights in District 10 was the most profitable condo resale transaction during the week of Oct 13 to 20.

The seller of the 4,047 sq ft unit on the fifth floor netted a profit of around $3.58 million (31.9%) when it fetched $14.8 million ($3,657 psf) on Oct 15. It was purchased for $11.22 million ($2,773 psf) in May 2011, resulting in an annualised gain of 1.8% over a holding period of more than 15 years.

Despite the seven-figure profit, it is still far below the condo’s all-time record gain of $4.7 million from a 2022 deal. That transaction involved a 4,951 sq ft duplex penthouse that changed hands for $23 million after it had been purchased for $18.3 million in June 2011.

Tomlinson Heights is a 70-unit boutique condo located on Tomlinson Road, off Paterson Road. Completed in 2014, the freehold development comprises a single residential tower housing three- and five-bedders measuring between 2,745 and 4,047 sq ft. It also has a pair of 4,951 sq ft duplex penthouses.

URA data compiled by EdgeProp Research shows that Tomlinson Heights recorded just two other resale deals this year, both of which were profitable. The units, each spanning 2,745 sq ft, posted gains of $800,000 and $2 million.

Another District 10 development, Leedon Residence , ranked second on the week’s list of most profitable condo transactions.

A 2,659 sq ft, four-bedroom unit garnered a profit of about $3.05 million (63.4%) when it was sold on Oct 16 for $7.85 million. The seller had bought the unit for $4.8 million in February 2014. That works out to a gain of 3.9% when annualised over a holding period of nearly 13 years.

The deal ranks as Leedon Residence’s sixth most profitable transaction, based on caveats lodged. The biggest profit stands at $5.2 million, from the resale of a 4,704 sq ft, duplex five-bedder on Feb 23. It changed hands for around $14 million after the owner had purchased it for $8.8 million in February 2017.

Completed in 2015, Leedon Residence is a 381-unit freehold development on Leedon Heights . It features two- to five-bedroom units, including garden suites and sky penthouses, ranging from 1,044 to 8,051 sq ft.

Excluding the Oct 16 and Feb 23 deals, the condo has logged 13 other resale transactions so far this year, all of which were in the black. Those units were sold for between $2.8 million and $14.3 million, netting profits ranging from $387,028 to $3.75 million.

Meanwhile, the steepest loss among condo resales during the week in review involved a four-bedder at Reflections at Keppel Bay .

The transaction left the seller nearly $2.02 million (28.7%) in the red, which translates to an annualised loss of 1.7% over a 19-year holding period. The 2,928 sq ft unit on the first floor was sold for $5.03 million ($1,716 psf) on Oct 16, after it had been bought in August 2007 for $7.04 million ($2,406 psf).

Still, this pales in comparison with the record loss at the District 4 condo. The seller of a 3,993 sq ft four-bedder incurred the largest shortfall of $4.13 million when it changed hands for $5.85 million in April 2022, down from its initial purchase price of $9.98 million.

Reflections at Keppel Bay is a 99-year leasehold development located along Keppel Bay View. Completed in 2011, it houses 1,129 units across one- to four-bedroom layouts, with sizes ranging from 732 to 4,919 sq ft.

Telok Blangah MRT Station is within a 10-minute walk, while retail and lifestyle amenities at VivoCity mall are a five-minute drive away.

title: Freehold project The Draycott tops weekly record price highs with $2,801 psf sale
article:
The Draycott — a freehold development in prime District 10 — led the list of non-landed private residential developments that posted a new psf-price peak during the week of Oct 13 to 20.

The project’s fresh record of $2,801 psf was set with the sale of a 2,637 sq ft three-bedder on the 29th floor for $7.39 million on Oct 16.

That is the first time an apartment at The Draycott has transacted above the $2,800 psf threshold. It surpasses the previous price high of $2,723 psf, established by the resale of another 2,637 sq ft three-bedder for $7.18 million on July 28.

Completed in 1980, The Draycott is one of Singapore’s earliest and most distinctive developments, located on Draycott Park. It comprises a 34-storey, tri-cylindrical tower housing 132 apartments, as well as four-storey blocks with two-bedders and maisonettes.

Resale psf prices at the development have trended steadily upwards over the past decade, according to a tabulation of caveats by EdgeProp Singapore . Its one-year average resale price has risen by more than 30% over the past decade, from $1,731 psf in October 2016 to about $2,345 psf as of October this year.

Coming in second on the list of top project highs for the week is Lentor Modern . The 99-year leasehold development achieved a new price peak of $2,606 psf with the sub-sale of a 1,109 sq ft, three-bedroom apartment for nearly $2.89 million on Oct 14.

The record-breaking sale inches past Lentor Modern’s former record of $2,596 psf, which came from a 732 sq ft two-bedder that fetched $1.9 million earlier this year on May 6.

Located in the Lentor Hills estate, Lentor Modern is an integrated development comprising 605 residential units across three 25-storey towers above a commercial podium. Completed in 2025, it has one- to four-bedroom units measuring between 527 and 1,528 sq ft.

In terms of absolute price, the most expensive transaction at the development thus far is the sub-sale of a 1,528 sq ft four-bedder, which fetched $3.85 million ($2,519 psf) on May 4.

In contrast to the week’s fresh price highs, only one project registered a new psf-price low.

At freehold condo Peak Residence , a 560 sq ft, one-bedroom unit set a new low of $2,189 psf when it changed hands for $1.23 million on Oct 19.

It is below Peak Residence’s previous low of $2,295 psf, which was set when an 829 sq ft two-bedder was purchased from the developer for $1.9 million in February 2023.

Completed last year, the 90-unit boutique project is located on an elevated site along Thomson Road in District 11. Two- and three-bedders, ranging from 775 to 1,087 sq ft, make up the majority of its unit mix. It also has one-bedders measuring between 527 and 560 sq ft, and 10 four-bedroom units spanning 1,389 sq ft each.

The latest deal marks the development’s inaugural resale transaction and its first caveated transaction since 2023. That year, the developer sold 45 units at Peak Residence at an average price of $2,509 psf.

title: November 2026: 3 Temasek-Linked Blue Chips to Watch
article:
Three of Singapore’s best-known companies have two things in common: they share the same major shareholder, and this year, they also share the same headwind.
The conflict in the Middle East has reached all three businesses.
It just hits each one differently.
All three report results in the first half of November, so it helps to know what to look for.
Temasek
, a global investment company headquartered in Singapore, holds sizeable stakes in each company.
Company
Temasek stake
As at
Reporting date
CapitaLand Investment
(SGX: 9CI)

Can CapitaLand Investment keep its fee engine running?
CapitaLand Investment Limited
(SGX: 9CI), or CLI, is a global real asset manager that earns fees from managing funds and properties.
Those fees are growing.
For the first half of 2026 (1H2026), fee-related revenue rose 20% year on year (YoY) to S$687 million.
Higher fees and lower finance costs helped operating PATMI grow 13% to S$293 million.
Group revenue actually slipped 2% to S$1.0 billion after CLI deconsolidated Synergy and divested a China business park.
Here’s the thing: event-driven fees supplied much of that growth.
Listed Funds Management revenue climbed 45% to S$224 million, largely from these fees.
Fees like these come and go.
On 4 November, watch whether recurring fees can carry growth on their own.
Lodging is the softer spot.
The segment’s EBITDA margin narrowed to 20% from 27% a year ago.
Revenue per available unit (RevPAU) in the Middle East, Africa, Türkiye and India declined 3% as geopolitical tensions weighed on these markets.
Don’t expect a dividend on 4 November: CLI pays only a first and final dividend.
It paid S$0.120 per share for FY2025 in May 2026.
Related articles:
S$10,000 to Invest: 3 Dividend Stocks I Would Consider Today
CICT, CLI and Wilmar on the Hot Seat: What You Should Expect Next
Will fuel costs weigh on SIA’s next dividend?
Singapore Airlines Limited (SGX: C6L), or SIA, runs Singapore Airlines and low-cost carrier Scoot.
It also owns 25.1% of the Air India Group.
SIA isn’t short of customers.
In the first quarter of the fiscal year ending 31 March 2027 (1QFY2027), revenue rose 19.3% YoY to a record S$5.7 billion.
Passenger yields improved 12%, and cargo revenue rose 33.3% as cargo yields climbed 28.1%.
SIA swung to a net loss of S$75.8 million from a profit of S$186.1 million a year ago.
So why the loss?
One word:
fuel
.
Jet fuel prices spiked after the Middle East conflict broke out on 28 February 2026, and SIA’s net fuel expenses rose 78.5%, or S$991 million.
A wider share of losses from Air India added to the strain.
On the flip side, cash is still coming in.
Free cash flow was about S$810 million.
As at 30 June 2026, SIA held S$9.1 billion in cash and bank balances against S$10.7 billion of debt.
Its debt-to-equity rose to 0.65 times from 0.62 times three months earlier.
SIA declares dividends only alongside its half-year and full-year results.
If the 11 November release covers the half year, we’ll find out whether SIA pays one.
Any payout will tell you how SIA weighs a loss-making quarter against positive free cash flow.
Management has already warned that fare adjustments cannot fully offset elevated fuel prices.
Related articles:
Singapore Airlines Shares Have Recovered. What Could Go Wrong Next?
SATS and SIA: How US$100 Oil Is Threatening the 2026 Aviation Recovery
Can SATS turn volume growth into cash?
SATS Ltd
(SGX: S58) handles air cargo and ground services through Gateway Services and runs catering through Food Solutions.
Volumes are growing.
In 1QFY2027, which ended on 30 June 2026, revenue rose 11.3% YoY to S$1.7 billion.
Cargo processed grew 8.6% to 2.6 million tonnes.
However, profit lagged.
Operating profit climbed 6.8% to S$133.8 million, but the operating margin narrowed to 8.0% from 8.3%.
SATS pointed to Middle East disruption to cargo flows and inflationary pressure.
Net profit rose just 6% to S$75.1 million as earnings from associates and joint ventures fell 18.9%.
Free cash flow is the lifeblood of dividends, so this is the number to watch.
It came in at negative S$22.6 million.
SATS put weaker operating cash flow down to working capital timing.
The next release will test that explanation.
SATS carried S$4.2 billion of debt as at 30 June 2026, with gross debt-to-equity at 1.41 times.
It did not disclose its cash balance.
SATS also did not declare a dividend for the quarter, the same as a year ago.
Management has warned that higher oil prices and Middle East tensions could bite harder in coming quarters.
